title: Our Planetary System
intro: Learn the solar system as one family of worlds: the Sun that holds almost all the mass, the four rocky terrestrial planets and the four giant jovian planets, their moons and rings, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, the Kuiper belt and the Oort cloud. Then see how the shared patterns of motion (and the exceptions) point to a common birth, and how flybys, orbiters, landers and sample-return missions have taught us all of this.

learningObjectives.text: Place the Sun, the eight planets, the asteroid belt, the Kuiper belt and the Oort cloud on a map of the solar system, and explain why one picture cannot show true sizes and distances.
Compare terrestrial and jovian planets by size, density, composition, surface, moons and rings.
Compare Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars by their atmospheres, surface conditions and evidence of past activity.
Compare Jupiter and Saturn (gas giants) with Uranus and Neptune (ice giants), including their rings.
Tell asteroids, comets and dwarf planets apart, and say where each is found.
Use the patterns of motion, and the exceptions to them, to reason about how the solar system formed.
Describe how flybys, orbiters, landers and sample-return missions work, and match each to a science goal.
Explain why the Sun holds almost all of the solar system's mass and where its energy is produced.
Describe the Galilean moons, Titan, Triton and Earth's Moon, and explain why our Moon is surprising.
State the three tests for a planet and use them to explain why Pluto is a dwarf planet.

sections.title: A map of the solar system

img.alt: The Sun, a huge glowing ball on the right, with the eight planets and the dwarf planets Pluto and Eris drawn at the same relative scale so they look tiny beside it.

steps.title: Eight planets, one huge Sun
bullets: The solar system is the **Sun** plus everything its gravity holds: eight **major planets**, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids, comets and dust.
The eight planets travel on nearly circular orbits. **Dwarf planets** such as Pluto and Eris are smaller, and some of them have quite stretched-out (elliptical) orbits.
Drawn to one size scale, the planets are specks beside the Sun. Even Jupiter, the biggest planet, is only about 1/10 of the Sun's width.

img.alt: Two maps side by side: on the left the inner solar system with the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and on the right the Kuiper belt around the planets' orbits and the vast spherical Oort cloud around everything.

steps.title: Belts and clouds beyond the planets
bullets: The **asteroid belt** is a doughnut of rocky bodies between Mars and Jupiter, about 2 to 3.5 AU from the Sun.
The **Kuiper belt** is a wider doughnut of icy bodies beyond Neptune's orbit, about 30 to 50 AU out.
The **Oort cloud** is a huge, roughly spherical shell of icy bodies at the far edge of the solar system, from about 2,000 to 100,000 AU.
1 AU (astronomical unit) is the average Earth-Sun distance, about 150 million km.

img.alt: A line running outward from the Sun on a logarithmic scale, marking the planets, the edge of the Sun's wind bubble, Voyager 1, the Oort cloud and the nearest stars, with distances in astronomical units.

steps.title: Why distances need a log scale
bullets: Neptune is 30 AU out, but the Oort cloud reaches about 100,000 AU. To fit both on one line, each tick mark is 10 times farther than the last. This is a **logarithmic scale**.
On such a map all eight planets crowd into the first part of the line, even though the gaps between them are huge in real life. Spacing on a log map is not a measurement of true distance.

Voyager 1, launched in 1977, has left the Sun's wind bubble (the heliosphere) and is in interstellar space. It is still nowhere near the Oort cloud: it needs roughly 300 years just to reach its inner edge.

img.alt: A column of planet photographs at their relative sizes: Mercury, Venus, Earth with its Moon, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

steps.title: Comparative planetology: learn by comparing
bullets: **Comparative planetology** means understanding one world by comparing it with others, much like learning about a person by meeting their family and friends.

It asks: How are Earth and the other planets alike and different? What makes a planet habitable, and why did life not start on the others? Which processes run across the solar system, and how do they affect Earth? How did the solar system, and Earth, form?
The same method now helps us make sense of planetary systems around other stars.

boxes.text: Why does a to-scale map look so empty? Space is mostly empty. The planets are tiny compared with the gaps between them, so no single picture can show both true sizes and true distances.
Going outward from the Sun: rocky planets, asteroid belt, giant planets, Kuiper belt, Oort cloud. Rock near the Sun, ice far away.

A picture with enlarged planets and neat spacing is not to scale, so it cannot be used to compare both sizes and distances. 'Nearly circular orbits in nearly the same plane' describes the eight planets, not every dwarf planet: Eris, for example, has a stretched-out, tilted orbit (see the Eris picture in the dwarf planets part). Slide 4 gives the belts as 2 to 3.5 AU (asteroids) and 30 to 50 AU (Kuiper) and the Oort cloud as 2,000 to 100,000 AU.

sections.title: The Sun: nearly all of the mass

img.alt: A pie chart of the solar system's mass that is almost entirely the yellow Sun slice, with Jupiter and Saturn as thin slivers beside it.

steps.title: The Sun is almost the whole solar system
bullets: The Sun holds more than **99.8%** of the solar system's mass. Planets, moons, asteroids and comets together add up to only about 0.2%.
Jupiter has about 1/1000 of the Sun's mass, and it is roughly 2.5 times as massive as all the other planets together. So all the planets combined are still only about 1/1000 of the Sun's mass.
That is why the Sun's gravity rules the whole system: it sets the orbit of every planet.

img.alt: A photograph of the whole Sun dotted with dark sunspots, next to a close-up of a huge streamer of hot gas leaping off the Sun with a tiny Earth added for size.

steps.title: What the Sun is made of
bullets: The Sun is a ball of hot, ionized gas: about 73% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass. Its visible surface is about 5500 °C (5800 K).
Its radius is 109 times Earth's and its mass is 333,000 times Earth's. It rotates about once every 27 Earth days.
**Sunspots** look dark only because they are cooler than the gas around them, and they can be big enough to swallow several Earths.

steps.title: Where the Sun's energy comes from
bullets: The Sun is a **nuclear fusion** power plant. Fusion happens only in the **core**, where temperature and pressure are enormous. The visible surface (photosphere) and the thin layers above it only let the energy out.
Each second the Sun turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into about 596 million tonnes of helium. The 'missing' 4 million tonnes or so becomes energy through E = mc^2.

The result is a **luminosity** of 3.8 x 10^26 W. Even losing over 4 million tonnes every second, the Sun has so much hydrogen that it has shone for almost 5 billion years and will shine about 5 billion more.
Sunlight sets the temperatures of the planets' surfaces and atmospheres. Planets and moons shine only by reflecting it.

boxes.text: Why does fusion happen only in the core? Fusing hydrogen nuclei needs extreme temperature and pressure. Both rise steadily with depth, and only the core is hot and dense enough.
Planets together = about 1/1000 of the Sun. Fusion = core only. The Sun is 99.8% of the mass, but it is not solid: it is gas all the way through.

'Where does nuclear fusion occur in the Sun?' The answer is the core, not the photosphere, chromosphere, corona or convection layer. 'If we combined all the planets, their mass would be about ___ the Sun's mass' is 1/1000 (not double, half, 1/10 or equal). Slide 7 gives 73% hydrogen and 25% helium; Cosmic Perspective 7.1 says 98% hydrogen and helium together. They agree.

sections.title: Terrestrial and jovian worlds

img.alt: Two photo panels: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars on the left, and Saturn, Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune on the right, all labelled, with the right-hand group far larger.

steps.title: Two families of planets
bullets: The four **terrestrial planets** (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small, rocky, dense and close to the Sun. 'Terrestrial' means Earth-like.
The four **jovian planets** (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are much larger, far from the Sun, and made mostly of hydrogen, helium and hydrogen compounds. 'Jovian' means Jupiter-like.
The Moon is rocky and shares Earth's orbit, so planetary scientists sometimes count it as a fifth terrestrial world. It is not a planet.

steps.title: Side-by-side properties
bullets: Terrestrial: smaller size and mass, higher density, rock and metal, a solid surface, few or no moons, no rings, warmer surfaces.
Jovian: larger size and mass, lower density, mostly hydrogen and helium and hydrogen compounds, no solid surface, many moons, rings, cold cloud tops.
Density is the clearest split: Earth is 5.5 g/cm3 and Saturn is 0.7 g/cm3. A jovian planet is huge but light for its size.
Moons: Mercury 0, Venus 0, Earth 1, Mars 2 tiny ones. Each jovian planet has dozens, and Saturn has close to 300.

steps.title: Gas giants and ice giants
bullets: Jupiter and Saturn are the **gas giants**: mostly hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune are the **ice giants**: they also contain much more water, ammonia and methane, which are hydrogen compounds.
'Gas' and 'ice' are only labels. Deep inside, the pressure is so high that the material is no longer an ordinary gas, and the 'ices' of Uranus and Neptune are hot fluids, not frozen solids.
All four count as jovian: each is mostly hydrogen and hydrogen compounds, with no solid surface, rings and many moons.
Judge a planet by several properties together. Venus is almost Earth's size but has a hostile surface, and Uranus and Neptune differ from Jupiter and Saturn.

boxes.text: Why are there two families? Near the young Sun it was hot, so only rock and metal could form solid grains. Farther out ices could freeze too, giving far more material to build big planets that could then hold on to hydrogen and helium. The next unit builds this story.
Terrestrial = Tiny, Tough (solid) and Toasty. Jovian = Jumbo, no solid surface, with Jewellery (rings) and loads of moons.

'Which is NOT a characteristic of all the terrestrial planets?' The trap option is 'They have substantial atmospheres': Mercury has almost none and Mars has a thin one. 'Which is NOT a characteristic of the jovian planets?' The false option is 'higher average densities than the terrestrial planets': jovian planets are LESS dense. Rings belong to all four jovian planets. Table 7.2 in the textbook has the full side-by-side list.

sections.title: The four terrestrial planets

img.alt: Mercury shown as a grey cratered globe with a close-up of a crater field, a table of its size, day length and temperatures, and an inset of yellow patches of water ice near its north pole.

steps.title: Mercury: the planet of extremes
bullets: Mercury is the smallest planet (0.38 Earth radii, 0.055 Earth masses) and the closest to the Sun. It has almost no atmosphere, so nothing spreads the heat around.
Surface temperatures swing from about 425 °C in daylight to about -170 °C at night: the biggest day-night difference of any planet.
The surface is cratered like the Moon, with long steep cliffs (scarps). Water ice survives in craters near the poles that never see sunlight.
Its density is high for such a small planet (5.4 g/cm3), which tells us it has a very large iron core.
One sunrise-to-sunrise day lasts 176 Earth days, twice its 88-day year, because Mercury spins exactly three times for every two orbits.

img.alt: Venus shown as a pale cloud-covered globe beside a radar-style view of its volcanic surface, a table of its size and temperature, and an inset of Venus shining as a bright morning star over the horizon.

steps.title: Venus: Earth's size, a very different world
bullets: Venus is Earth's near twin in size and mass: 95% as wide and 81.5% as massive.
A thick carbon dioxide atmosphere, about 100 times the mass of Earth's, hides the surface. Cloud-penetrating radar shows volcanoes, mountains and craters underneath.
An extreme **greenhouse effect** keeps the whole surface at about 470 °C, day and night. Venus is hotter than Mercury even though it is farther from the Sun.
Venus rotates very slowly and **backward** compared with its orbit direction (once in 243 Earth days), so the Sun would rise in the west.
It shines as the bright 'Morning Star' (or evening star) near sunrise or sunset.

img.alt: Earth shown as a blue globe with swirling clouds, a table of its size, day, year and temperature range, and a small picture of Earth beside the much smaller Moon at the correct relative sizes.

steps.title: Earth: the only known living planet
bullets: Earth is the **densest** planet in the solar system (5.5 g/cm3), the only world known to host life and the only one known to have liquid water on its surface.
Temperatures run from about -90 °C to 60 °C and average about 15 °C, thanks to a moderate greenhouse effect.
Its Moon is surprisingly large: about 27% of Earth's diameter. Mercury and Venus have no moons and Mars has two tiny ones.
Life has been present for about 85% of Earth's history, but our species has existed for only the last 0.007% of it.

img.alt: Mars shown as a rusty orange globe beside a picture of the huge volcano Olympus Mons, a table of its size and temperatures, and an elevation map of water-carved channels coloured by height.

steps.title: Mars: a frozen desert with a wet past
bullets: Mars is about half Earth's width and about 10% of its mass. Iron oxide (rust) dust makes the surface orange-red.
The air is very thin (far lower pressure than on top of Mount Everest), surface temperatures run from about -110 °C to 35 °C, and the polar caps hold frozen carbon dioxide and water.

Dried-up riverbeds, rock-strewn floodplains and minerals that form in water show that liquid water once flowed on Mars, and conditions may then have suited life. The big flows probably ended at least 3 billion years ago.

Mars has **Olympus Mons**, the largest volcano in the solar system, and a canyon that runs nearly one-fifth of the way around the planet (Valles Marineris). Its two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, may be captured asteroids.
You still could not walk on Mars without a spacesuit: the air pressure is far too low, there is almost no oxygen, it is bitterly cold, and no ozone layer blocks ultraviolet light.

boxes.text: Why is Venus so hot when Earth is not? Venus's thick carbon dioxide blanket traps heat so well that night brings no relief. Earth has the same gas, but only enough for a moderate greenhouse effect. Comparing the two shows how much an atmosphere matters.

Why does Mercury's density point to a big iron core? A small planet is squeezed only a little by its own gravity, so a density as high as 5.4 g/cm3 means it must be made of much denser material than Earth's average: lots of iron.
Mercury = extremes (biggest day-night swing, no air). Venus = hottest average (greenhouse). Earth = densest, liquid water, life. Mars = once wet, now cold and thin.

'Which planet is most similar in size and mass to Earth?' Venus (not Mars or Mercury). 'Most extreme difference between day and night temperature?' Mercury, not Venus: Venus is equally hot everywhere. 'Which indicates that Mars could once have supported life?' Dried-up riverbeds, floodplains and water-formed minerals, not its volcanoes, polar caps, moons or the number of spacecraft sent there. 'Which world could you visit without a spacesuit?' None except Earth: Mercury, Venus, the Moon and Mars all need one.

sections.title: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune

img.alt: Jupiter shown as a banded orange and white globe with the huge Great Red Spot, a table of its size, day length and temperature, and a glowing infrared image of the planet.

steps.title: Jupiter: the giant of giants
bullets: Jupiter is the largest planet in size and mass: 11 times Earth's radius, 318 Earth masses, nearly 2.5 times the mass of all the other planets combined, yet only about 1/1000 of the Sun's mass.
It is mostly hydrogen and helium, with thick cloud layers and storms (the Great Red Spot could swallow two or three Earths). There is no solid surface: a probe sinks until pressure crushes it.
Jupiter also spins fastest: a day lasts only 9 h 55 min. A year lasts 11.86 Earth years, and cloud tops are near -145 °C.
It has around 100 known moons (the count keeps rising), including the four big Galilean moons, and a thin, faint ring.

img.alt: Saturn shown as a pale yellow globe with its broad rings, a table of its size, day length and temperature, and a hazy orange picture of its largest moon, Titan.

steps.title: Saturn: the ringed, low-density planet
bullets: Saturn is the second-largest planet: 9.4 Earth radii and 95 Earth masses. Its average density, 0.7 g/cm3, is lower than water's (1.0).
Low gravity and density plus a fast spin (10 h 32 min a day) squish it: it is about 10% wider than it is tall.
It has the most spectacular ring system (though not the only one) and the most moons of any planet, close to 300, including the cloudy giant **Titan**.
Like Jupiter it is mostly hydrogen and helium, with no solid surface. A year lasts 29.45 Earth years.

img.alt: Uranus shown as a pale blue-green globe with thin rings circling it almost vertically, a table of its size and day length, and an infrared telescope image showing its bright rings.

steps.title: Uranus: the planet on its side
bullets: Uranus is an **ice giant**: hydrogen and helium plus water, ammonia and methane. Methane gives it a pale blue-green colour. It is 4 Earth radii wide and 14.5 Earth masses.

Its axis is tilted about 98 degrees (the same tilt is sometimes quoted as 82 degrees, measured from the other direction), so it rolls around the Sun on its side and spins backward compared with most planets.
That tilt gives the most extreme seasons of any planet: each pole gets about 42 years of continuous sunshine, then about 42 years of darkness.
It has the second-most visible rings after Saturn (dark and narrow) and at least 27 moons. Only Voyager 2 has visited it, in 1986.

img.alt: Neptune shown as a pale blue globe with faint cloud streaks, a table of its size and day length, and a deep blue processed image of the planet from Voyager 2.

steps.title: Neptune: Uranus's blue twin
bullets: Neptune is a physical and chemical twin of Uranus, except that its axis is not tipped on its side. It is slightly smaller (3.9 Earth radii) but slightly more massive (17.1 Earth masses) because it is denser (1.64 g/cm3).
It looks deep blue in the famous Voyager 2 picture, but that image was processed. In real colour Neptune is similar to Uranus.
It is the farthest planet, 30 AU from the Sun, with a year of 165 Earth years. Only Voyager 2 has visited it, in 1989.
Its large moon **Triton** orbits backward and is thought to be a captured Kuiper belt object.

boxes.text: Why does Uranus look blue-green? Methane gas in its atmosphere absorbs red light, so the light that comes back to us is blue-green.
Gas giants = Jupiter and Saturn. Ice giants = Uranus and Neptune. By size: Jupiter > Saturn > Uranus > Neptune, but Neptune is slightly MORE massive than Uranus.

'The most massive planet?' Jupiter, not Saturn. 'Which planets have a ring system?' All four jovian planets, so the answer is 'all of the above', not just Saturn. 'Uranus's large axis tilt causes it to...' have extreme seasonal variations (not very short days, very hot, very cold, or one side always facing the Sun). Slide 12 lists about 115 moons for Jupiter and slide 14 about 300 for Saturn, while the textbook (2022 counts) gives 79 and 82; counts keep rising, so remember only that the jovian planets have many more moons than the terrestrial ones. Slide 16 quotes Uranus's tilt as 82.23 degrees and Table 7.1 as 97.9 degrees: the same tilt measured from opposite directions.

sections.title: Moons: worlds in their own right

img.alt: A black chart of selected moons grouped under their planets, with Earth drawn at the right for size; Jupiter and Saturn have the longest columns of moons.

steps.title: Jovian planets have far more moons
bullets: Mercury and Venus have no moons, Earth has one and Mars has two tiny ones. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune have dozens each, and Saturn has close to 300.
Most of those moons are small chunks, but a few are giant worlds with their own geology. Some are larger than Mercury.
Most large moons orbit in their planet's equatorial plane, in the same direction the planet spins. That is one of the patterns used to work out how the solar system formed.

img.alt: Four photographs of Jupiter's biggest moons side by side: yellow-orange Io, pale cracked Europa, grey and brown Ganymede and dark cratered Callisto.

steps.title: Jupiter's four Galilean moons
bullets: Galileo found Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto in 1610. In the picture they run left to right in order of distance from Jupiter.
**Io** is the most geologically active object in the solar system, with erupting volcanoes.
**Europa** has an icy surface and possibly a liquid water ocean hidden underneath.
**Ganymede** is the largest moon in the solar system, even larger than Mercury.
**Callisto** is a heavily cratered, geologically dead 'ice ball'.

img.alt: A strip with the Sun at the right and the planets drawn to the same scale, with names of well-known moons listed under each planet: Moon, Phobos and Deimos, Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto, Titan, Enceladus, Triton and others.

steps.title: Other notable moons
bullets: **Titan** (Saturn) is the only moon with a thick atmosphere. Its surface is about -180 °C, with rivers and lakes of liquid methane and ethane. **Enceladus** (Saturn) sprays ice fountains from its southern hemisphere.
**Triton** (Neptune) is larger than Pluto and has nitrogen geysers. It is the only large moon that orbits backward, so it was probably captured.
**Charon** (Pluto) is about half of Pluto's width, so big that the pair is almost a double world.
**Phobos and Deimos** (Mars) are two tiny, lumpy moons that may be captured asteroids. Earth's own Moon is large for its planet (see the exceptions).
Rank by what a body orbits, not by size. Ganymede and Titan are both larger than Mercury, but they are moons because they circle a planet, not the Sun.

boxes.text: Why is Io volcanic when our Moon is not? Jupiter's gravity keeps squeezing and stretching Io as it moves along its orbit, which heats its inside enough to power volcanoes. A moon's geology depends on its own heating and history, not just on its size.
Galilean moons in order from Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto. 'I Eat Gummy Candy.' Io = volcanoes, Europa = ocean, Ganymede = biggest, Callisto = craters.

'Which planet is orbited by Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto?' Jupiter, not Saturn. Ganymede is the largest moon. Our Moon is not the largest (it is about fifth), and Titan, not any other moon, has the thick atmosphere. The tidal-heating explanation of Io is not on the slides; it is only needed for the reason, not for the exam fact that Io is the most volcanic world.

sections.title: Rings of the giant planets

img.alt: An artist's painting of Saturn's rings up close, with countless chunks of blue-white ice of different sizes drifting in a thin sheet above the planet's golden clouds.

steps.title: Rings are swarms of orbiting chunks
bullets: Saturn's rings look like solid sheets from far away, but they are made of countless small chunks of ice and rock.
Each piece orbits Saturn like a tiny moon. The pieces range from dust grains to blocks as big as a city block.
A ring is not attached to the planet. It is a flat crowd of independent orbits.

img.alt: A long strip view of Saturn's rings from the inner edge outward, showing many thin ring bands separated by dark gaps, with the Colombo Gap, the Maxwell Gap, the C ring and the B ring labelled.

steps.title: Wide but unbelievably thin
bullets: The ring system is enormously wide but extremely thin. To be as thin compared with its width, a sheet of paper would have to be about 2.8 km long.
The rings divide into many thin ringlets separated by dark gaps, such as the Colombo and Maxwell gaps. The C ring and the B ring are two of the main bands.
The thinness is why the rings seem to vanish when we see them edge-on from Earth.

steps.title: Every giant planet has rings
bullets: Saturn's rings are the only ones that are easy to see, but Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune also have ring systems.
Jupiter's ring is thin and faint, Uranus's rings are dark and narrow (the second most visible after Saturn's), and Neptune's rings are dark too.
The terrestrial planets have no rings.
Voyager 2 helped find and study the rings by looking back at them with the Sun behind them. That view is possible only from beyond the planet.

boxes.text: Why do the rings look solid? From far away the countless pieces blend into a smooth sheet, just as a beach of fine sand looks like one surface from a plane.
A ring is a river of tiny moons. Rings = all four jovian planets. Saturn = the bright ones.

'Which of the following planets has a ring system? Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, or all of the above?' The answer is all of the above. A ring is never a solid disk, and 'jovian planet' does not mean 'solid all the way through'. The thinness comparison (a 2.8 km sheet of paper) is from slide 15.

sections.title: Dwarf planets: Pluto, Eris and more

steps.title: What makes a planet, and what makes a dwarf planet?
bullets: In 2006 astronomers agreed on three tests. A **planet** (1) orbits the Sun, (2) is massive enough for its own gravity to pull it into a nearly round shape, and (3) has **cleared its orbital neighborhood** of other sizable bodies.
A **dwarf planet** passes tests 1 and 2 but fails test 3. It is also not a moon. There are eight planets.

For 75 years Pluto counted as the ninth planet. Then Eris was found in 2005, a little more massive than Pluto, and dozens of other objects turned out to be not much smaller. Counting them all would have made the planet list very long.
The deciding factor was Pluto's small size and mass. It is too small to dominate its orbital zone. Its great distance, its large moon Charon and its ice-and-rock make-up were not what decided it.

img.alt: Pluto as seen by New Horizons, a pale tan and white globe, beside a telescope image labelling Pluto and its moons Charon, Nix, Hydra, P4 and P5.

steps.title: Pluto and its big moon Charon
bullets: Pluto is an icy, comet-like world, round but small: radius 1185 km (0.19 Earth radii), mass about 0.2% of Earth's, density 1.9 g/cm3, surface near -230 °C.
It orbits at 39.5 AU on average and takes 248 Earth years to go around the Sun. It lives in the **Kuiper belt**, not in the asteroid belt or the Oort cloud.
Pluto has five known moons. The largest, Charon, is about half of Pluto's width, so big that the two circle a point between them and always show each other the same face.
The New Horizons spacecraft flew past Pluto in 2015.

img.alt: A diagram of the planets' orbits with the very stretched-out, tilted orbit of Eris swinging far outside the orbits of Neptune and Pluto, and Eris marked near the bottom.

steps.title: Eris, Ceres and other dwarf planets
bullets: **Eris** is the most massive dwarf planet, yet it is still about 20 times less massive than Mercury. It is the most massive object in the Kuiper belt region, and its orbit is far more elongated and tilted than any planet's.
**Ceres** is the largest object in the asteroid belt and counts as a dwarf planet: round, but surrounded by thousands of other asteroids. The Dawn spacecraft orbited it from 2015 to 2018.
Other known dwarf planets include Haumea and Makemake, and astronomers expect many more in the distant outer solar system.
Dwarf planets are small: the whole group is a tiny part of the solar system's mass.

boxes.text: Why does 'clearing the neighborhood' matter? A true planet's gravity dominates its orbital zone, pulling in or flinging away smaller bodies over time. Pluto shares its zone with many similar Kuiper belt objects, so it dominates nothing.
Planet = three yeses: orbits the Sun, is round, has cleared its orbit. Dwarf planet = two yeses and a NO on 'cleared its orbit'. Moon = orbits a planet instead.

'What was important in classifying Pluto as a dwarf planet?' Its small size and mass, not its distance, its moon Charon or its composition. 'In what region is Pluto found?' The Kuiper belt. 'Which dwarf planet is most massive?' Eris, not Pluto. Slide 18 says Charon is 'only slightly smaller than Pluto itself'; by width it is about half of Pluto, so treat it as 'unusually large for a moon'. The three planet tests are not written on the slides; they come from the 2006 International Astronomical Union definition.

sections.title: Asteroids, comets, and the distant icy realms

img.alt: Four grey rocky bodies in a row labelled Ceres 939 km, Vesta 525 km, Pallas 512 km and Hygiea 434 km, with Ceres the largest and roundest.

steps.title: Asteroids: rocky and metallic leftovers
bullets: **Asteroids** are small rocky or metallic bodies. Most orbit in the **asteroid belt** between Mars and Jupiter, about 2 to 3.5 AU from the Sun, where there are likely about a million objects wider than 1 km.
The four largest are Ceres (939 km), Vesta (525 km), Pallas (512 km) and Hygiea (434 km). Ceres, the largest, is a dwarf planet. Most asteroids are far smaller and not round.
There are many asteroids, but the belt is mostly empty space. The bodies are separated by great distances, so it is not a crowded ring of planet-sized objects.

steps.title: Comets: icy bodies from the cold outskirts
bullets: **Comets** are small bodies made mostly of ices (water, ammonia, methane) mixed with dust and rock.
Most comets stay far away in the Kuiper belt or the Oort cloud and never come near the Sun. Only a rare few plunge into the inner solar system.

When a comet nears the Sun, heating makes gas and dust escape, forming a fuzzy **coma** around the nucleus and a **tail**. The tail points away from the Sun, pushed by sunlight and the solar wind, even while the comet is moving toward the Sun.
Far from the Sun a comet has no coma and no tail at all.

img.alt: A top view of the outer solar system with the Sun in the middle and the positions of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune marked, surrounded by many coloured dots for small rocky and icy bodies gathered in rings and clumps.

steps.title: Swarms are not random
bullets: Asteroids and comets are not scattered evenly. They gather in three distinct regions: the asteroid belt (rocky), the Kuiper belt (icy) and the Oort cloud (icy).

The **Kuiper belt** lies beyond Neptune, about 30 to 50 AU out, in a doughnut shape. It holds at least 100,000 icy bodies wider than 100 km and about 100 times the mass of the asteroid belt. Pluto and Eris are its largest known members.

The **Oort cloud** is a vast, roughly spherical shell from about 2,000 to 100,000 AU, with possibly a trillion or more comets and icy planetesimals. Its comets come from every direction, which is why it is a sphere and not a flat ring.

An Oort cloud comet is the farthest from the Sun of anything in this unit: asteroid belt (2 to 3.5 AU), Neptune (30 AU), Pluto (about 40 AU), Kuiper belt comet (30 to 50 AU), Oort cloud comet (thousands of AU).

steps.title: Asteroid or comet? The difference that matters
bullets: The major difference is composition: asteroids are rocky or metallic, comets are icy.
A tail is not the test. A comet shows a tail only near the Sun; farther out it is a dark, icy lump. Size is not the test either.
Location is a clue: asteroids mostly orbit between Mars and Jupiter, comets mostly live in the Kuiper belt and Oort cloud.

boxes.text: Why are asteroids rocky and comets icy? Near the young Sun only rock and metal could stay solid, while farther out it was cold enough for ice to freeze too. Where a body formed, and still lives, decides what it is made of.
Asteroids: rock, between Mars and Jupiter. Comets: ice, Kuiper belt and Oort cloud. A comet's tail always points AWAY from the Sun.

'Asteroids never have tails and comets always have tails' and 'asteroids are smaller than comets' are wrong options: the real difference is rocky versus icy. The Oort cloud is not a cloud of gas, not a belt in the planets' plane, and not between Mars and Jupiter; it is a roughly spherical region beyond Pluto's orbit that may hold a trillion comets. A comet in the Oort cloud is farther from the Sun than Neptune, Pluto or an asteroid-belt asteroid. Slide 5 says 'trillions'; the textbook says 'a trillion'.

sections.title: Patterns that reveal the system's history

img.alt: A top view of the solar system: a yellow Sun in the middle and a red planet on a circular orbit, with curved arrows showing that the orbit and the planet's own rotation go the same way.

steps.title: Pattern 1: orderly motion
bullets: All planets orbit the Sun in the **same direction** (counterclockwise seen from above Earth's north pole), on nearly circular orbits in nearly the **same flat plane**.
Most planets also rotate in that same direction, with fairly small axis tilts. The Sun's own rotation goes the same way.
Most large moons orbit in their planet's equatorial plane, in the same direction that the planet rotates.

steps.title: Patterns 2 and 3: two kinds of planets, and swarms of small bodies
bullets: Small, rocky, dense planets sit close to the Sun and big, hydrogen-rich planets sit farther out. The change is sharp, not gradual.
Asteroids and comets are not scattered at random. They are concentrated in the asteroid belt, the Kuiper belt and the Oort cloud.
A good explanation of the solar system must account for both facts: why rock is inside and gas giants are outside, and why small bodies gather in these regions.

steps.title: What the patterns say: the nebular hypothesis
bullets: The **nebular hypothesis** says the solar system formed from a cloud of gas and dust that collapsed under gravity. As it shrank it spun faster and flattened into a rotating **disk**, with the young Sun at the centre.
A spinning flat disk gives the shared plane and direction of Pattern 1. Material in the disk collided and clumped into **planetesimals**, which grew into planets and smaller bodies.
The disk was hot near the Sun and cold far away, so rock and metal formed close in while ices could also form farther out. That fits Pattern 2 and explains why comets are icy.

Astronomers can test this by looking at young stars: telescopes show flattened disks of gas and dust, and planetary systems apparently in the process of forming, in many clouds, including the Orion Nebula.

steps.title: Test a model with many observations
bullets: A successful model has to explain the shared orbital pattern, the difference between inner and outer planets, and the small-body reservoirs. One similarity alone is not enough.
It must also leave room for the exceptions (next section) and make predictions that we can check against other planetary systems.
Observation first: spot the pattern. Explanation next: decide which formation process could produce it.

boxes.text: Why does a rotating disk give one shared direction and plane? When a cloud collapses, its spin keeps going the same way. A spinning cloud flattens into a disk, and everything that forms inside it circles in the direction of the spin, in the plane of the disk.
Same direction, same plane, same spin: if all the orbits match, think 'born in one rotating disk'.

'Which is NOT a pattern of motion in the solar system?' The false statement is 'The planets orbit the Sun in a direction opposite to the Sun's rotation': they orbit the SAME way the Sun rotates. Also true: most planets rotate the way they orbit, most orbits lie in the same plane, and most large moons orbit in their planet's spin direction. 'Have astronomers seen clouds that look like planetary systems forming?' Yes: many, including the Orion Nebula. The detailed formation story belongs to the next unit.

sections.title: Exceptions to the patterns

img.alt: Uranus as a pale blue-green disk with thin rings circling it almost vertically, so the planet seems to lie on its side.

steps.title: Uranus is tipped on its side
bullets: Most planets spin with their axes fairly upright (Earth's tilt is 23.5 degrees). Uranus's axis is tilted about 98 degrees, so it rotates on its side.
Its rings and major moons share the sideways tilt. A huge collision while it was forming may explain it.
The tilt gives Uranus the most extreme seasons of any planet: each pole has about 42 years of sunlight and then about 42 years of night.

img.alt: Venus as a yellow-brown globe covered with mottled surface markings in a false-colour radar-style view.

steps.title: Venus and Uranus rotate backward
bullets: Most planets rotate in the same direction in which they orbit. Venus rotates the opposite way (retrograde), very slowly: one turn takes 243 Earth days, and the Sun rises in the west.
Venus still orbits the Sun in the same direction as every other planet, and in the same plane. Only its spin is backward, and it is slow, not fast.
A tilt above 90 degrees means Uranus also spins backward compared with most planets.

img.alt: Earth, a large blue and white globe, beside the much smaller grey Moon drawn at the correct relative sizes.

steps.title: Earth's Moon is surprisingly large
bullets: The Moon is about 27% of Earth's diameter (a little over a quarter) and about 1/80 of its mass. Almost every other moon is a much smaller fraction of its planet.
It is not the largest moon in the solar system (Ganymede is bigger than Mercury), but it is the one that is unusually large for its planet.
The other terrestrial planets have no moon (Mercury, Venus) or just two tiny ones (Mars). The leading idea is that the Moon formed from a giant impact early in Earth's history.

steps.title: Other oddities, and why exceptions are clues
bullets: Triton is the only large moon that orbits its planet backward (opposite to Neptune's rotation), which points to a body that formed elsewhere and was captured.
Many small moons have unusual, tilted or backward orbits.
An exception is not a failure of the pattern. A good theory must explain the general rule and also leave room for special events such as collisions and captures.

boxes.text: Why do exceptions matter? The rules suggest the planets formed together in one disk, so a body that breaks a rule probably had a special history: a collision (Uranus's tilt, the Moon) or a capture (Triton). Exceptions help us decide which special events happened.
Three planetary exceptions: Uranus = tilted onto its side, Venus = backward slow spin, Earth = oversize Moon.

'What is unusual about Venus?' It ROTATES in the opposite direction to its orbit. It does not orbit backward, orbit in a different plane, orbit too fast or rotate fast; it spins very slowly. 'What is surprising about Earth's Moon?' Its size relative to its planet, not its craters, its distance or its lack of atmosphere. Do not mix up Uranus's tilted AXIS with a tilted ORBIT: its orbit is in the usual plane.

sections.title: How spacecraft explore other worlds

img.alt: The Apollo lunar module standing on the grey Moon with an astronaut next to it.

steps.title: What goes into a mission
bullets: Space travel is complex, scientifically and administratively. Someone must propose the mission (what will it accomplish?), plan its milestones, decide who designs and builds which parts, and pay for it (is the science worth the cost?).
Many agencies fly missions: NASA (USA), ESA (Europe), CSA (Canada), ISRO (India), CNSA (China) and Roscosmos (Russia), among others.
Engineers also have to choose fuel and propulsion, landing and sample-collection equipment, scientific instruments, and backups in case something fails. Crewed missions add life support.
Robotic spacecraft carry computers, power (for example solar cells), propulsion, instruments and radios. They mostly follow preprogrammed commands plus updates from Earth, and most never come back.

steps.title: Match the mission to the question
bullets: A **flyby** passes a target once and can survey many objects, but its close observation window is brief.
An **orbiter** circles a world for repeated measurements and broad mapping, but reaching and holding orbit needs extra fuel.
A **lander** or **rover** makes direct surface measurements. They are detailed but limited to a small region, and the landing has to succeed.
A **sample return mission** brings material to laboratories on Earth. It is the hardest robotic type, because the spacecraft must also get back home.

steps.title: Remote sensing and direct measurements
bullets: Cameras and spectrographs measure reflected or emitted light from a distance. Radar sees through thick clouds, which is why it is so useful at Venus and Titan.
Landers and rovers examine local conditions directly. Probes that fly into an atmosphere measure it on the way down.
A spacecraft's gravity tug from a world also reveals that world's mass and density, something Earth-based telescopes cannot measure so well.
Mission design always balances science goals, communication delay, power, travel time, hazards and cost.

boxes.text: Why use spacecraft when we have telescopes? Spacecraft get close, so their pictures and spectra are far sharper than any telescope's. They can also feel a world's gravity, look back at rings lit from behind, and sample the surface or atmosphere directly.
Flyby: a brief pass. Orbiter: repeated global views. Lander or rover: local surface evidence. Sample return: a round trip.

A photograph alone cannot replace composition measurements or direct surface analysis; each method has limits. The teacher's slides also list the cost and scheduling questions (budget, planning, failure modes): they are part of why choosing the mission type depends on both science goals and money.

sections.title: Flybys and orbiters

img.alt: Left: a spacecraft picture of Pioneer 11 against the starry Milky Way. Right: the Voyager 1 spacecraft with its dish antenna and long boom, on a white background.

steps.title: Flybys: pass once, cheap, short look
bullets: A **flyby** passes a world just once and carries on. It never has to slow down, so it needs less fuel, weighs less and costs less to launch.
The drawback is time: a flyby studies the target for a much shorter time than an orbiter does.
Flybys can still do a lot. Close up, their cameras and spectrographs beat the biggest telescopes, and a target's pull on the spacecraft reveals its mass.
Pioneer 11 made the first flyby of Saturn. The two Voyagers (launched in 1977) have left the planets far behind and are travelling through interstellar space.

img.alt: A diagram of Voyager 2's path curving past Jupiter in 1979, Saturn in 1981, Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989, over circles marking the planets' orbits.

steps.title: Voyager 2 and the gravitational slingshot
bullets: One flyby can visit several worlds. Voyager 2 passed Jupiter (1979), Saturn (1981), Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989).

At each planet it used the planet's gravity as a **gravitational slingshot**, which bends the path and can add speed by borrowing a tiny bit of the planet's orbital energy. New Horizons used a Jupiter flyby to gain about 20% in speed and reach Pluto more than 3 years sooner.
Voyager 2 is still the only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus and Neptune.

img.alt: Three spacecraft pictures labelled Galileo at Jupiter, Cassini above Saturn's rings and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter above the Martian surface.

steps.title: Orbiters: stay and study
bullets: An **orbiter** goes into orbit around a world, so it has more time to gather data than a flyby. It can follow an atmosphere, a magnetic environment and a surface over the long term and map them again and again.
Drawbacks: it needs extra fuel to slow down and enter orbit, so it costs more than a flyby, and it is restricted in collecting samples or seeing precise surface detail.
Examples: Galileo (first to orbit Jupiter), Cassini (Saturn, 2004 to 2017) and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (Mars). Orbiters have visited every planet except Uranus and Neptune.
Galileo and Cassini were deliberately sent into Jupiter and Saturn at the end of their missions, so they could never crash into, and contaminate, a moon that might host life.

steps.title: Flyby or orbiter? The trade-off
bullets: Choose a flyby for a tight budget, a quick first look, or one trip past several targets.
Choose an orbiter for years of repeated measurements of one world.

Mars orbiters save fuel by aerobraking: they enter a long, stretched orbit and then skim the thin martian air at the low point of each pass, slowing a little each time until the orbit is small and circular.

boxes.text: Why is a flyby cheaper? Launch cost depends mostly on weight, and fuel is a big part of a spacecraft's weight. In space there is no air drag, so a spacecraft needs fuel only to change its trajectory. A flyby never has to slow down, so it carries less fuel.
Flyby = quick look, many targets, cheap. Orbiter = long look, one target, dearer.

'A significant drawback of a flyby compared with an orbiter?' It studies the planet for a much shorter time. It does not reach the planet slower, carry worse instruments or stay farther away. The teacher's flyby table lists Juno, but Juno has orbited Jupiter since 2016, so it belongs with the orbiters. The year column on slides 6 and 8 mixes launch dates (Pioneer 11, 1973) with arrival dates (Galileo, 1995), and Cassini reached Saturn in 2004, not 2005.

sections.title: Landers, probes, sample return and humans

img.alt: A close-up self-portrait of the Curiosity rover on the rusty-brown Martian surface, showing its wheels, mast and instrument arm.

steps.title: Landers and rovers: close up, but local
bullets: A **lander** touches down on a world's surface. A **rover** is a wheeled lander that can explore a wider area. They study rock and soil, weather and local conditions, and can run experiments and collect samples.

Strength: very detailed, direct measurements. Limit: a small area only, and the landing must succeed. Mars rovers include Curiosity (arrived 2012) and Perseverance (2021), which also carried the Ingenuity helicopter.
Landers have reached the Moon, Venus, Mars and Saturn's moon Titan, as well as a few asteroids and a comet.

On the jovian planets there is no solid surface to land on, so spacecraft send **atmospheric probes** instead. The Galileo probe sent data from Jupiter's clouds for about an hour before heat and pressure destroyed it.

img.alt: Four pictures in order: a spacecraft entering Mars's atmosphere, a parachute opening, rockets slowing the craft above the ground, and a sky crane lowering the rover while the rocket stage flies away.

steps.title: Landing softly is the hard part
bullets: Curiosity and Perseverance used a four-step landing: (1) friction with the atmosphere slows the spacecraft, (2) a parachute slows it to about 350 km/h, (3) rockets bring it to a halt just above the ground while a sky crane lowers the rover on a tether, (4) the tether is released and the rocket stage flies off to crash a safe distance away.
Mars's air is thin, so a parachute is not enough on its own, and rockets must finish the slowing down.

img.alt: Two photographs of the orange-brown surface of Saturn's moon Titan, with rounded cobbles on a flat plain, next to a photograph of the Huygens probe, a round capsule.

steps.title: Combination missions
bullets: Some missions combine spacecraft types to get both broad and close-up views. Viking 1 and 2 each took an orbiter and a lander to Mars.

**Cassini-Huygens**: the Cassini orbiter studied Saturn, its rings and its moons from 2004 to 2017, and carried the **Huygens** probe, which landed on Titan in 2005 and photographed a pebble-strewn plain carved by liquid methane.
**Galileo** at Jupiter was an orbiter that also dropped a probe into the atmosphere.

img.alt: An astronaut in a white spacesuit and gold visor standing on the grey, dusty surface of the Moon.

steps.title: Sample return and human spaceflight
bullets: A **sample return mission** lands, collects samples, blasts off and flies home. It is much more complicated than a flyby or orbiter because of the return trip, but labs on Earth can analyze the samples in far greater detail than any instrument that fits on a spacecraft.
Samples so far have come from the Moon, a few asteroids and a comet's dust. A sample return from Mars is a major goal for the future.

**Human spaceflight** is the most complicated type, because the crew must survive: food, water, medicine and oxygen, protection from extreme heat, cold and radiation, the biological effects of weightlessness, and no easy help if something goes wrong (as with Apollo 13).
Humans have set foot on only one other world, the Moon, and not since 1972.

boxes.text: Why is landing so hard? A spacecraft arrives at thousands of km/h and must slow to nearly zero in a few minutes, using a thin atmosphere, a parachute and rockets, with no way to correct a mistake. A flyby never has to do that.
Flyby: one pass. Orbiter: stays. Lander: touches down. Sample return: touches down and comes home. Human: all of that, plus keeping people alive.

'Why would a lander be a bad idea at a jovian planet?' Because the jovian planets have no solid surface to land on, not because they are too far away or have nothing interesting. 'Which worlds have humans visited?' Only the Moon (the last time in 1972). The year column in the slide tables is not always an arrival date (Cassini is listed as 2005, but it reached Saturn in 2004), so rely on the textbook dates: Cassini at Saturn 2004 to 2017, Huygens on Titan 2005, Galileo probe 1995.
