At least 27 moons, dark narrow rings
Deep, with water, ammonia and methane
At least 14 moons, dark faint rings

cards.back: A relatively small, rocky, dense planet of the inner solar system with a solid surface and few or no moons: Mercury, Venus, Earth or Mars.
A large outer planet with no solid surface, made mostly of hydrogen, helium and hydrogen compounds, with rings and many moons: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Neptune.
Jupiter or Saturn: a giant planet made mostly of hydrogen and helium, with no solid surface.
Uranus or Neptune: giant planets with much more water, ammonia and methane than Jupiter or Saturn. The 'ices' are hot fluids deep inside, not frozen solids.
A small rocky or metallic body orbiting the Sun; most are in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.
An ice-rich small body, mostly ice mixed with dust and rock, that releases gas and dust to form a coma and tail when heated near the Sun.
cards.short: Icy body that can grow a coma and tail.

cards.back: A doughnut-shaped region beyond Neptune, about 30 to 50 AU out, with many icy bodies (including Pluto and Eris) and about 100 times the asteroid belt's mass.
A vast, roughly spherical shell of icy bodies from about 2,000 to 100,000 AU, possibly holding a trillion comets; the source of many comets that come from every direction.
A body that orbits the Sun and is massive enough to be nearly round, but has not cleared its orbital neighborhood and is not a moon (for example Pluto, Eris, Ceres).
cards.short: Round, but has not cleared its orbit.

cards.back: The model that the solar system formed from a collapsing, rotating cloud of gas and dust that flattened into a disk, with the Sun at the centre and planets growing in the disk.
cards.short: A rotating disk formed from a collapsing cloud.

cards.back: A mission that passes a target once and continues on. Cheaper than other missions, but with much less time to gather data.
A spacecraft that goes into orbit around a world for long-term, repeated observations. It needs more fuel than a flyby and cannot collect samples.
A spacecraft that reaches a world's surface and makes close-up measurements at one location; a rover lets it explore more widely.
The study of worlds by comparing their similarities and differences to test explanations for their histories and processes.
cards.short: Learn about worlds by comparing them.

cards.back: The region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, about 2 to 3.5 AU from the Sun, holding most asteroids; roughly a million objects wider than 1 km, spread over a huge volume.
cards.short: Rocky region between Mars and Jupiter.

cards.back: More than 99.8% of the solar system's mass is in the Sun. All the planets together are only about 1/1000 of the Sun's mass.
Hydrogen nuclei fusing into helium in the Sun's core, turning over 4 million tonnes of mass into energy every second (E = mc^2). It happens only in the core.
cards.short: Hydrogen to helium in the core.

cards.back: Heating of a planet's surface by an atmosphere that traps heat. Moderate on Earth, extreme on Venus (about 470 °C everywhere).
cards.short: Atmosphere traps heat; extreme on Venus.

cards.back: Spinning in the direction opposite to the one most planets rotate and orbit. Venus (very slowly) and Uranus (tilted over 90 degrees) rotate this way.
cards.short: Spin opposite to the usual direction.

cards.back: The angle between a planet's spin axis and the line perpendicular to its orbital plane. Earth's is 23.5 degrees; Uranus's is about 98 degrees, giving extreme seasons.
cards.short: Spin axis angle: Uranus about 98 degrees.

cards.back: Jupiter's four largest moons, discovered by Galileo: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
Jupiter's innermost Galilean moon and the most volcanically active world in the solar system.
A Galilean moon with an icy surface and a possible liquid water ocean beneath it, a promising place to look for life.
cards.short: Icy moon with a possible ocean.

cards.back: Jupiter's largest moon and the largest moon in the solar system, bigger than Mercury.
cards.short: Largest moon in the solar system.

cards.back: The outermost Galilean moon: a large, old, heavily cratered, geologically dead 'ice ball'.
Saturn's largest moon and the only moon with a thick atmosphere. Its frigid surface (about -180 °C) has lakes and rivers of liquid methane and ethane.
Neptune's largest moon, larger than Pluto. It orbits backward, opposite to Neptune's rotation, so it was probably a Kuiper belt object that Neptune captured.
Pluto's largest moon, about half of Pluto's width: so big that Pluto and Charon are almost a double world.
About 27% of Earth's diameter: unusually large compared with its planet. Most other moons are much smaller relative to their planets.
Flat swarms of countless separate chunks of ice and rock, each orbiting like a tiny moon. All four jovian planets have them; Saturn's are by far the most visible.
cards.short: Orbiting chunks of ice and rock.

cards.back: The most massive dwarf planet, about 20 times less massive than Mercury, with a very elongated, tilted orbit in the Kuiper belt region.
The largest object in the asteroid belt (939 km wide) and a dwarf planet; the Dawn spacecraft orbited it from 2015 to 2018.
cards.short: Dwarf planet in the asteroid belt.

cards.back: A dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt made of ice and rock, with five known moons. It was called the ninth planet for 75 years until it was reclassified because of its small size and mass.
A planet's gravity dominating its orbital zone, so that other sizable bodies have been pulled in or flung away. Planets do it, dwarf planets do not.
A body that orbits the Sun, is massive enough to be nearly round, and has cleared its orbital neighborhood. There are eight.
The fuzzy cloud of gas and dust around a comet's nucleus, released when sunlight heats the comet near the Sun.
Gas and dust pushed away from the Sun by sunlight and the solar wind. The tail points away from the Sun, not necessarily behind the comet's path.
cards.short: Always points away from the Sun.

cards.back: The orderly motions of the large bodies: the planets orbit in the same direction in nearly the same plane, most rotate that way too, and most large moons orbit in their planet's spin direction.
cards.short: Same direction, same plane, same spin.

cards.back: A spacecraft that descends into an atmosphere instead of landing, as the Galileo probe did at Jupiter, which has no solid surface.
cards.short: Dives into a giant planet's atmosphere.

cards.back: A wheeled robot that travels over a world's surface to examine a wide area, such as Curiosity and Perseverance on Mars.
A round-trip mission that lands, collects material and brings it back to Earth for laboratory study. It is far more complicated than a flyby or an orbiter.
Using a planet's gravity to bend a spacecraft's path and speed it up, which saves fuel. Voyager 2 used it at each giant planet.
cards.short: A planet's gravity gives a boost.

cards.back: A Saturn mission: the Cassini orbiter studied Saturn, its rings and moons (2004 to 2017), and the Huygens probe landed on Titan in 2005.
The only spacecraft to visit Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989), after flybys of Jupiter (1979) and Saturn (1981).

quiz.q: A diagram enlarges all planets but preserves their order from the Sun. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The planet order is shown, but the drawn sizes or gaps may not represent actual scale.
The gaps between every neighboring orbit are equal.
The sizes and distances are both accurately represented.
The asteroid belt must be denser than the rings of Saturn.
quiz.why: A schematic can preserve the order of bodies while changing sizes or distances so the objects can be seen. Real gaps are far from equal (Neptune is 30 AU out, Mars 1.5 AU), and nothing in the picture says the asteroid belt is denser than Saturn's rings.

quiz.q: Which observation best supports classifying Earth with the terrestrial planets rather than with the jovian planets?
options: It is a comparatively small, dense world with a rocky surface.
It has a moon that orbits it.
It travels around the Sun.
It reflects sunlight into space.
quiz.why: Rocky composition, small size, a solid surface and high density are the defining traits of the terrestrial family. Having a moon, orbiting the Sun and reflecting sunlight are true of jovian planets as well, so they cannot separate the two families.

quiz.q: A student groups Uranus with Jupiter because both are enormous compared with Earth. What important distinction should be added?
options: Uranus is an ice giant, while Jupiter is a gas giant.
Uranus is a terrestrial planet, while Jupiter is a dwarf planet.
Uranus orbits beyond the Kuiper belt, while Jupiter is inside the asteroid belt.
Uranus has no atmosphere, while Jupiter has one.
quiz.why: Both are giant (jovian) planets, but Uranus and Neptune hold much more water, ammonia and methane, while Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium. Uranus orbits at about 19 AU, well inside the Kuiper belt (30 to 50 AU), and Jupiter orbits beyond the asteroid belt; neither is terrestrial or a dwarf planet, and both have deep atmospheres.

quiz.q: Two planets have similar radii, but one has a dense carbon-dioxide atmosphere and a far hotter surface. Which inference is strongest?
options: Similar size alone does not determine a planet's surface environment.
Their surface conditions must be identical because their sizes are similar.
The denser atmosphere proves the hotter planet formed farther from the Sun.
The hotter planet cannot be terrestrial.
quiz.why: Venus and Earth illustrate that comparable size does not guarantee similar atmospheric or surface conditions: Venus's thick carbon dioxide gives it a 470 °C surface. Venus is nearer the Sun than Earth, not farther, and it is a terrestrial planet.

quiz.q: A cratered world has almost no atmosphere to redistribute heat. Which additional observation would best fit Mercury?
options: Large temperature contrasts between its day and night sides.
Clouds that hide nearly all surface features.
A global ocean beneath a thick atmosphere.
A tail that always points along its orbit.
quiz.why: With almost no atmosphere, Mercury cannot spread heat around: its surface swings from about 425 °C by day to about -170 °C at night. Clouds, oceans and a thick atmosphere describe other worlds, and tails belong to comets.

quiz.q: Which evidence most directly supports the claim that Mars had flowing liquid water in its past?
options: Surface channels and minerals associated with water-altered environments.
Its current surface temperature is always above water's boiling point.
Its two small moons are made of ice.
Its orbit is nearly circular.
quiz.why: Dried-up riverbeds, floodplains and water-formed minerals preserve evidence for ancient water even though liquid water is not broadly stable on the surface today. Mars is cold, not hot, its moons are rocky, and a circular orbit says nothing about water.

quiz.q: A probe detects many narrow ring features around a giant planet. What is the best physical interpretation?
options: The rings consist of many separate particles orbiting the planet.
The rings are a single rigid sheet attached to the planet.
The rings are the planet's solid surface viewed edge-on.
The rings are trails left by planets that escaped the system.
quiz.why: Planetary rings are made from large numbers of separate pieces of ice and rock, each orbiting like a tiny moon. They are not a rigid sheet, and the giant planets have no solid surface.

quiz.q: A body is round and orbits the Sun, but many sizable objects share its orbital region. Which classification best fits?
options: Dwarf planet
Major planet
Moon
Comet
quiz.why: A dwarf planet can be round and orbit the Sun without clearing its orbital neighborhood. A major planet must clear its orbit, a moon orbits a planet, and a comet is an irregular icy body that need not be round.

quiz.q: Why can a comet become much more visible as it approaches the Sun?
options: Heating releases gas and dust that create a coma and tails.
Its orbital speed converts its whole body into visible light.
The Sun pulls it into a permanent ring.
Its surface turns into a liquid ocean.
quiz.why: Solar heating causes volatile material to escape from an icy comet, producing a coma and tails that reflect sunlight. The comet is not turned into light, pulled into a ring or turned into an ocean.

quiz.q: A comet's tail points away from the Sun even while the comet is moving toward the Sun. What does this show?
options: Tail direction is not simply the direction opposite to the comet's motion.
The comet must be orbiting backward.
The comet's tail is a solid extension of its nucleus.
All comet tails point behind the comet's orbital path.
quiz.why: Sunlight and the solar wind push tail material away from the Sun, so the tail need not trail the comet's motion. A tail is not solid, and the comet is not orbiting backward.

quiz.q: Which pairing of small-body population and location is most accurate?
options: Kuiper belt: beyond Neptune
Asteroid belt: beyond the Oort cloud
Oort cloud: between Earth and Mars
Kuiper belt: inside Mercury's orbit
quiz.why: The Kuiper belt is a population of icy objects beyond Neptune (about 30 to 50 AU). The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter, and the Oort cloud is the farthest region of all.

quiz.q: A long-period comet approaches the inner solar system from a highly extended orbit. Which distant source is most strongly associated with such comets?
options: The Oort cloud
The asteroid belt
Saturn's rings
The terrestrial planets
quiz.why: The distant, roughly spherical Oort cloud is inferred to supply many comets that arrive from random directions on very long orbits. Asteroids and rings are rocky or icy pieces that do not behave this way.

quiz.q: Which pattern is most consistent with planets forming in a rotating disk?
options: Most planets orbit in nearly the same plane and direction.
Every planet has the same orbital period.
All moons orbit in exactly the same plane as their planet.
Every planet rotates at the same rate.
quiz.why: A rotating, flattened disk naturally produces coordinated orbital directions and a shared orbital plane. Periods and rotation rates differ from planet to planet, and some moons have unusual orbits.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly describes the nebular hypothesis?
options: A rotating cloud of gas and dust collapsed and flattened into a disk from which the Sun and planets formed.
The planets formed independently and were later captured into random orbits by the Sun.
The Sun formed first as a solid object and later split into the planets.
Comets collided to create the gas cloud that became the Sun.
quiz.why: The model begins with a collapsing, rotating cloud that forms a central Sun and a surrounding disk. Random capture would not give shared orbit directions, and the Sun is a gas ball, not a solid object that split.

quiz.q: Why does the nebular model predict rocky planets closer to the Sun and icy material farther out?
options: The early disk had a temperature gradient that affected which materials could condense.
The Sun's gravity only affected rocky material near its surface.
Icy objects cannot orbit inside the asteroid belt today.
The outer planets formed before the Sun began to shine.
quiz.why: Temperature varied across the disk (hot near the Sun, cold far away), so different materials could condense in different regions. Gravity acts on all material, and the ordering is about where things formed, not about timing.

quiz.q: A model explains the shared orbital plane but cannot explain why the inner planets are rocky and the outer planets are giant worlds. What is the best scientific response?
options: Treat the model as incomplete and test a mechanism that explains both patterns.
Ignore the compositional evidence because one pattern already fits.
Change the observations until they match the model.
Conclude that all planets formed independently.
quiz.why: A useful formation model must account for multiple independent patterns, not just one. Ignoring evidence or altering observations is not science, and independent formation would not explain the shared orbital plane.

quiz.q: A spacecraft must map a planet repeatedly over several years. Which mission design best fits that goal?
options: Orbiter
Flyby
Atmospheric entry probe with no transmitter
One-time impactor
quiz.why: An orbiter can make repeated measurements and survey a world from many viewing angles. A flyby passes once, a probe lasts minutes to hours, and an impactor makes a single event.

quiz.q: A mission needs high-resolution measurements of soil chemistry at one safe landing site. Which approach is most direct?
options: Lander or rover
Distant flyby only
Telescope on Earth
A second planet's moon
quiz.why: A lander or rover can directly analyze the local surface, although it samples only a limited area. A flyby or an Earth telescope cannot measure soil chemistry in place.

quiz.q: Why might scientists choose a flyby instead of an orbiter for a mission to several small bodies?
options: A flyby can visit multiple targets without carrying the fuel needed to orbit each one.
A flyby provides continuous global mapping of each target for years.
A flyby can collect surface samples without approaching a target.
A flyby removes communication delays.
quiz.why: Flybys trade long-duration coverage for the ability to encounter multiple targets with a simpler trajectory and less fuel. They do not map for years, collect samples without approaching, or remove communication delay.

quiz.q: A thick atmosphere prevents a camera from seeing the surface clearly. Which method could provide complementary surface information?
options: Radar remote sensing or measurements from a probe that enters the atmosphere.
A visible-light image from a farther distance.
A measurement of the planet's orbital direction only.
A telescope pointed at the planet's rings.
quiz.why: Radar can penetrate some cloud layers (as at Venus and Titan), and atmospheric probes can make measurements below the clouds. A visible-light image from farther away is no better, and orbital direction says nothing about the surface.

quiz.q: What is a key limitation of a rover compared with an orbiter?
options: It makes detailed measurements over a very limited surface area.
It cannot send any scientific data.
It observes only the planet's global magnetic field.
It must remain outside the atmosphere.
quiz.why: Surface missions provide local detail but cannot directly survey the entire planet. Rovers do send data, and they work inside the atmosphere on the surface.

quiz.q: A scientist compares the number of moons, surface geology, and atmospheric composition across several planets. What is the central purpose of this comparison?
options: To use similarities and differences to test explanations of planetary history.
To determine that planets with moons must be more massive than the Sun.
To prove that every world formed in a separate system.
To replace measurements with visual resemblance.
quiz.why: Comparative planetology tests hypotheses by examining patterns and exceptions among worlds. It relies on measurements, and it does not suggest that planets form in separate systems.

quiz.q: A spacecraft returns a rock sample, while an orbiter maps the full planet. Why are both missions scientifically useful?
options: The sample gives detailed local composition while orbital data supplies broad context.
The sample determines the entire planet's surface history by itself.
Orbital mapping reveals no information about surface features.
The two data types measure the same thing at the same scale.
quiz.why: Local analysis and global mapping are complementary forms of evidence: one is detailed but from one place, the other is broad but less detailed.

quiz.q: Which conclusion best combines the orbital and compositional patterns of the solar system?
options: A rotating, temperature-structured disk can explain both shared orbital motions and inner-to-outer composition differences.
The planets' common direction proves that all have identical compositions.
The locations of asteroids show that planets do not orbit the Sun.
The differences among planets rule out a common formation process.
quiz.why: The nebular model links the rotating disk's geometry with temperature-dependent material condensation. A shared direction says nothing about identical compositions, and differences among planets do not rule out a common origin.

quiz.q: A small rocky body orbits the Sun and is large enough for gravity to make it round, but many similar bodies share its orbital region. Which classification best fits?
options: A major planet, because being round is the only criterion.
A dwarf planet, because it has not cleared its orbital neighborhood.
A moon, because it is smaller than Earth.
An asteroid, because all rocky bodies are asteroids.
A comet, because its orbit contains other objects.
quiz.why: A dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is massive enough to be nearly round, but it has not cleared its orbital neighborhood. A major planet satisfies all three criteria, including clearing its orbital region.

quiz.q: What is surprising about Earth's Moon compared with the moons of the other planets?
options: It is unusually large compared with the planet it orbits.
It is the largest moon in the solar system.
It is the only moon that has an atmosphere.
It orbits Earth backward, opposite to Earth's spin.
It has more craters than any other moon.
quiz.why: The Moon's diameter is about 27% of Earth's, a far larger fraction than almost any other moon has compared with its planet. It is not the largest moon (Ganymede is bigger than Mercury), the thick atmosphere belongs to Titan, and the only large backward-orbiting moon is Triton.
quiz.source: Ch7.1 slide 10; Ch7.2 slide 6; Cosmic Perspective 7.2

quiz.q: Mercury is closer to the Sun than Venus, yet Venus has the hotter surface. Which explanation is best?
options: Mercury has a thick cloud layer that reflects most sunlight back to space.
Venus is larger than Mercury, and larger planets are always hotter.
Venus has a much bigger iron core that heats its surface from below.
Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, so its surface stays near 470 °C by day and night.
Venus rotates faster than Mercury, so sunlight is concentrated on its day side.
quiz.why: Venus's atmosphere is about 100 times the mass of Earth's and mostly carbon dioxide, so heat cannot escape and the whole surface stays near 470 °C. Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so it bakes at 425 °C by day and drops to about -170 °C at night. Venus actually rotates very slowly, and size or core cannot explain the temperature.

quiz.q: Mercury is much smaller than Earth, yet its average density (5.4 g/cm3) is almost as high as Earth's (5.5 g/cm3). What is the best inference?
options: Gravity squeezes Mercury's interior harder than Earth's, which raises its density.
Mercury contains a much larger fraction of dense iron than Earth does, so it must have a very large metal core.
Mercury is made mostly of ice, which is dense at very low temperatures.
Mercury is farther from the Sun than it looks, which makes it denser.
Mercury's thick atmosphere adds extra mass.
quiz.why: A small planet is squeezed much less by its own gravity than Earth is, so reaching nearly Earth's density means Mercury is made of denser material: it must have a very large iron core. Ice would lower the density, and Mercury has almost no atmosphere.

quiz.q: Saturn has about 95 times Earth's mass, but its average density is only 0.7 g/cm3, less than the 1.0 g/cm3 of water. What does this show?
options: Saturn is made mainly of rock and metal, just spread over a larger volume.
Saturn's rings add a large volume but almost no mass, which lowers its density.
A planet with a large mass must have a high density.
Saturn has a hollow region at its centre.
Saturn is made mostly of light gases (hydrogen and helium), so a large mass does not mean a high density.
quiz.why: Density is mass divided by volume. Saturn is enormous in volume but made mostly of hydrogen and helium, so its average density is below water's. Mass and density are different things, and all four jovian planets are less dense than the terrestrial planets.

quiz.q: Jupiter has about 2.5 times the mass of all the other planets combined, and about 1/1000 of the Sun's mass. What follows?
options: The Sun and Jupiter share the solar system's mass about equally.
The Sun holds only about half of the solar system's mass.
The planets together hold about 10% of the solar system's mass.
The Sun holds nearly all of the mass, and all the planets together are only about 1/1000 of it.
The planets together have more mass than the Sun's core.
quiz.why: Jupiter is about 1/1000 of the Sun's mass, and the other planets together add only about 0.4 of that, so all the planets total roughly 1/1000 of the Sun. The Sun holds more than 99.8% of the system's mass.

quiz.q: Which pairing of a Galilean moon with its main feature is correct?
options: Io: a heavily cratered, geologically dead ice ball
Callisto: the most volcanically active world in the solar system
Ganymede: a moon smaller than Mercury
Europa: an icy surface that may hide an ocean of liquid water
Europa: a thick atmosphere with lakes of liquid methane
quiz.why: Europa has an icy crust with a possible subsurface ocean. Io, not Callisto, is the volcanic world, and Callisto is the cratered ice ball. Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system and bigger than Mercury, and the methane lakes and thick atmosphere belong to Saturn's Titan.

quiz.q: Which of these statements about Pluto is NOT correct?
options: It orbits the Sun in the Kuiper belt.
It is made largely of ice and rock.
It has several moons, the largest being Charon.
It is the most massive dwarf planet.
It has not cleared the region around its orbit.
quiz.why: Eris, discovered in 2005, is slightly more massive than Pluto, so Pluto is not the most massive dwarf planet. The other statements are true: Pluto is a Kuiper belt body of ice and rock with five known moons, and it has not cleared its orbit, which is why it is a dwarf planet.

quiz.q: Which planet is correctly matched with its unusual feature?
options: Mars: a moon that is unusually large for its planet
Neptune: an axis tilted nearly 90 degrees, so it rolls on its side
Venus: a slow spin in the direction opposite to its orbit
Uranus: an orbit in a different plane from all the other planets
Mercury: an orbit around the Sun in the opposite direction
quiz.why: Venus rotates backward (very slowly) compared with its orbit direction, though it orbits the Sun the usual way. Earth, not Mars, has the large moon; Uranus, not Neptune, is tipped on its side; and Uranus's axis is tilted but its orbit is in the usual plane. Every planet orbits in the same direction.

quiz.q: A comet photographed far beyond Neptune's orbit shows no tail at all. What is the best explanation?
options: It is not a comet at all, because every comet always has a tail.
Comets that far out have lost all of their ice.
The solar wind is strongest beyond Neptune and blows tails away.
A tail forms only when the Sun heats the comet enough to release gas and dust, which happens near the Sun.
Tails always trail behind the comet's motion, so one pointing sideways cannot be seen.
quiz.why: A comet is an icy body, and its coma and tail appear only when sunlight heats it near the Sun. Far from the Sun it is a cold, dark lump. Tails do not last all the time, comets keep their ice until they are heated, and tails point away from the Sun, not along the orbit.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly compares the asteroid belt with the Kuiper belt?
options: Both are made mainly of ice, but the Kuiper belt is closer to the Sun.
The asteroid belt lies beyond Neptune and holds Pluto, while the Kuiper belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
The asteroid belt is rocky and metallic and lies between Mars and Jupiter; the Kuiper belt is icy, lies beyond Neptune and has about 100 times as much mass.
The Kuiper belt is a roughly spherical shell, and the asteroid belt is a flat ring beyond Neptune.
The asteroid belt has about 100 times the mass of the Kuiper belt, and both are rocky.
quiz.why: The asteroid belt (2 to 3.5 AU) holds rocky and metallic bodies between Mars and Jupiter. The Kuiper belt (30 to 50 AU) is a doughnut of icy bodies beyond Neptune with about 100 times the asteroid belt's mass and contains Pluto and Eris. The roughly spherical shell is the Oort cloud.

quiz.q: Triton, Neptune's largest moon, orbits Neptune in the direction opposite to Neptune's rotation. What does this most strongly suggest?
options: Triton formed together with Neptune in the same disk, like most large moons.
Neptune's rotation must have reversed after Triton formed.
Triton orbits backward because it is the most massive moon in the solar system.
Triton probably formed elsewhere, as a Kuiper belt object, and was captured by Neptune's gravity.
Triton was thrown out of Jupiter's moon system long ago.
quiz.why: Most large moons orbit in their planet's spin direction because they formed in a disk around it. A moon that orbits the other way almost certainly did not form there; Triton resembles a Kuiper belt object that was captured. Mass does not set an orbit's direction.

quiz.q: A mission must study Saturn's atmosphere and rings for several years and also examine the surface of Titan. Which combination fits best?
options: A single flyby spacecraft, because a flyby stays near its target for years.
A lander placed on Saturn itself, because Saturn has a solid surface.
An orbiter around Saturn that also carries a lander or probe for Titan, as in the Cassini-Huygens mission.
A sample-return spacecraft alone, since returning a Titan sample answers both goals.
Two separate flybys, since a flyby can land on a moon.
quiz.why: Years of repeated observations of Saturn and its rings need an orbiter. The surface of Titan needs a lander or probe. Saturn has no solid surface to land on, a flyby studies a target only briefly, and a flyby cannot land. Cassini orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017 and its Huygens probe landed on Titan in 2005.

quiz.q: Which observation gives the most direct support for the idea that planetary systems form from a rotating disk of gas and dust?
options: Venus rotates backward.
Earth has an unusually large Moon.
Telescopes show flattened disks of gas and dust around young stars in clouds such as the Orion Nebula.
Saturn has bright rings.
The Sun is much more massive than all the planets.
quiz.why: Seeing flattened disks around newborn stars, in star-forming clouds like the Orion Nebula, is a direct look at planetary systems in the act of forming. Backward rotation, a large moon, rings and the Sun's mass are all facts about our own system and do not show disks forming elsewhere.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Chapter 8 (outside the Ch7 slides)

order.title: Planets by distance from the Sun
order.prompt: Put the planets in order of average distance from the Sun, the closest at the bottom and the farthest at the top.
order.why: Distances: Mercury 0.39 AU, Venus 0.72, Earth 1.00, Mars 1.52, Jupiter 5.2, Saturn 9.5, Uranus 19.2, Neptune 30.1. The four terrestrial planets are close together; each jovian planet is much farther than the last.

order.title: Regions of the solar system
order.prompt: Put these regions in order of distance from the Sun, the closest at the bottom and the farthest at the top.
order.why: The terrestrial planets orbit within 1.5 AU, the asteroid belt lies at 2 to 3.5 AU, the jovian planets at 5 to 30 AU, the Kuiper belt at 30 to 50 AU, and the Oort cloud reaches from about 2,000 to 100,000 AU.

order.title: Planets by size
order.prompt: Put the planets in order of radius, the smallest at the bottom and the largest at the top.
order.why: Radius in Earth radii: Mercury 0.38, Mars 0.53, Venus 0.95, Earth 1.00, Neptune 3.9, Uranus 4.0, Saturn 9.4, Jupiter 11.2. Earth and Venus are almost twins, and so are Uranus and Neptune.

order.title: Planets by average density
order.prompt: Put these planets in order of average density, the least dense at the bottom and the densest at the top.
order.why: Densities in g/cm3: Saturn 0.70, Jupiter 1.33, Neptune 1.64, Mars 3.93, Venus 5.24, Mercury 5.43, Earth 5.52. The jovian planets are far less dense than the terrestrial ones, and Earth is the densest planet of all.

sort.title: Terrestrial planet, jovian planet or dwarf planet?
sort.prompt: Sort each item into the group it belongs to.

items.text: A small, dense world with a solid surface and few or no moons
A planet with no solid surface that has rings

sort.why: The four inner worlds are small, dense and solid; the four giants are large with no solid surface, rings and many moons. Pluto, Eris and Ceres are round but have not cleared their orbits, so they are dwarf planets.

sort.title: Planet, dwarf planet or moon?
sort.prompt: Sort each world by what it is. Remember: size alone does not decide it.

items.text: Charon, half the width of Pluto

sort.why: A major planet orbits the Sun, is round and has cleared its orbit. A dwarf planet fails the last test. A moon orbits a planet or dwarf planet, even if it is bigger than Mercury (Ganymede, Titan).

sort.title: Which kind of mission fits?
sort.prompt: Sort each description by the mission type it fits best.

items.text: Cheapest, because it never has to slow down
Cassini studying Saturn for more than a decade
Galileo circling Jupiter and its moons
Long-term data on a planet's atmosphere and magnetic field
Curiosity analyzing rocks in one crater
A spacecraft that must launch off a world and fly home
Measuring the soil at one landing site

sort.why: A flyby is cheap and quick and can visit several targets. An orbiter stays for years and maps a whole world. Landers, rovers and sample-return craft work at one surface location, and a sample-return craft must also get home.

sort.title: Asteroid belt, Kuiper belt or Oort cloud?
sort.prompt: Sort each fact by the region of the solar system it describes.

items.text: Rocky and metallic bodies between Mars and Jupiter
A doughnut of icy bodies beyond Neptune
About 100 times the mass of the asteroid belt
A roughly spherical shell of icy comets
Source of comets that arrive from every direction

sort.why: Rocky bodies in a belt between Mars and Jupiter are asteroids. The Kuiper belt is icy and lies beyond Neptune with Pluto and Eris. The Oort cloud is far larger, roughly spherical and the farthest region of all.
